claims.text: Controlled thermal oxidation can form a continuous, adherent, lubricious oxide layer on a high-entropy-alloy surface.
The thermally formed oxide layer will lower the coefficient of friction over a wide temperature range.
The thermally formed oxide layer will lower wear rate over a wide temperature range.
AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 or a similar Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti composition is a relevant high-entropy-alloy starting material.
The untreated starting surface has a native, non-optimized oxide layer.
A single-step oxidation treatment in air can promote in-situ formation of a protective lubricant oxide film.
The treatment can remain effective from room temperature to at least approximately 300 °C.
The treatment can remain effective under cyclic mechanical stresses.
The structural mediator is a thin, continuous, and adherent oxide layer.
The oxide layer may be enriched in Ti or Cr and contain TiO2 or Cr2O3.
The oxide layer is self-healing under operating conditions.
The preformed oxide acts as a solid lubricant by reducing shear stress during sliding.
The oxide provides a protective barrier that minimizes material removal.
Oxide stability across temperature is responsible for sustained self-lubrication.
Thermal oxidation is expected to reduce coefficient of friction by as much as roughly 50% relative to the untreated alloy.
Thermal oxidation is expected to reduce wear rate by at least one order of magnitude relative to the untreated alloy under identical loads.
An untreated, naturally oxidized alloy has higher friction and wear than the proposed thermally oxidized alloy.
The benefit persists only while the oxide layer remains continuous and adherent.
Oxide spallation or degradation under excessive mechanical stress or aggressive chemical exposure will diminish the improvement.
Prior evidence indicates that protective oxide layers enhance high-temperature wear resistance.

contradictions.description: The prediction says the friction reduction may be 'up to' roughly 50%, which permits smaller reductions, whereas the falsification rule demands approximately 50% lower friction across the tested range. The experiment could therefore reject outcomes that are consistent with the stated prediction.
